Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the chase! The floodlights are on and the players are already out in the middle now. Alyssa Healy and Georgia Voll are the two openers for Australia Women. It will be Kranti Gaud to start proceedings with the ball. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Right then, 281 was not enough in the first game, but will 292 be? India Women will hope so, but need a much better effort from their bowlers. They have changed tactics and gone with more seamers than in the previous match but need early wickets and, more importantly, to hold onto catches. India will be a bit relieved to see Phoebe Litchfield not playing, but Georgia Voll is no less of a threat at the top of the order. The Aussies chased down 282 with 35 balls to spare, and if we go by that, they will be confident of gunning this target down as well. Join us in a bit for the second essay.

Australia Women will be satisfied with the way their bowlers pulled things back after a difficult start. Ash Gardner was outstanding, keeping things tight while also striking twice at key moments. The Aussies backed it up with sharp fielding and safe catching, cutting off boundaries and saving runs in the deep. Once Tahlia McGrath dismissed Smriti Mandhana, the pressure was on, and the visitors never let it ease. Annabel Sutherland and Megan Schutt added a wicket each, but it was Darcie Brown who did the real damage, cleaning up the lower order and finishing the job.

The Indian openers once again underlined their consistency. Although they found it tough to keep the singles flowing, they compensated well by finding boundaries at regular intervals. The pair put on 70 runs for the opening stand, with Smriti Mandhana looking in sublime touch. She made the most of the conditions to register her 12th WODI century, reaching the landmark in just 77 deliveries - the second-fastest ton by an Indian in this format. But once she departed, the innings lost momentum as the middle order faltered yet again. Deepti Sharma contributed a steady 40, and Sneh Rana played a few lusty blows, but the finishing push was missing, much like in the first game.

From 180/3 at the 30-over mark to being bowled out for 292, India’s dependence on their top order was once again on display. Still, the total marked their highest-ever score against Australia in WODIs. The hosts will be a touch disappointed at missing out on the 300-run milestone, but they do have a competitive score on the board to work with.

Following a convincing victory for Australia in the opening match, the second ODI of the three-match series between India Women and Australia Women is set to be a high-stakes affair. The match will take place once again at the Maharaja Yadavindra Singh International Cricket Stadium in Mullanpur, New Chandigarh. With a 1-0 lead, Australia are on the verge of securing a series win, while India will be desperate to bounce back and level the series. The first ODI served as a wake-up call for the Indian team, particularly in the bowling and fielding departments. Despite a competitive total of 281 for seven, anchored by half-centuries from Pratika Rawal, Smriti Mandhana, and Harleen Deol, the bowlers failed to defend the score. Crucially, the Indian fielders dropped four catches, allowing key Australian batters to capitalise and guide their team to an eight-wicket victory. Phoebe Litchfield and Beth Mooney were the main beneficiaries of India's lapses in the field. The Indian spin quartet, consisting of Deepti Sharma, Shree Charani, Radha Yadav, and Sneh Rana, struggled to create pressure and failed to take wickets, with only Rana managing to claim a scalp.
